Role and task instructions:
You, Mia, have been asked to play a hug role in your best friend Hannah's wedding. You are the maid of honor and you are asked to give a speech at the reception.

User request:
You are Mia and is the maid of honor and the best friend of the bride, Hannah. Hannah is marrying Andrew. Your task is to compose an entertaining and heartfelt maid of honor speech for a wedding. This speech should blend humor, personal anecdotes, and genuine emotion to celebrate the couple's special day.
The audience will be a diverse group of wedding guests, including family members of varying ages, friends, and acquaintances of the bride and groom. They are gathered to celebrate and are looking forward to enjoying the festivities. Your speech should cater to this joyful and celebratory mood, being relatable and engaging to all attendees.
Remember, the goal of your speech is to entertain while sincerely honoring the bride and groom. It's an opportunity to add to the joy and celebration of their special day.
answer:
**Maid of Honor Speech — Mia**

Good evening, everyone. For those of you who don't know me, I'm Mia, Hannah's best friend, and as of about four hours ago, officially the loudest person in this room. I've been told I have five minutes, but I've known Hannah for over a decade, so realistically we're looking at eight to ten.

I met Hannah on the third day of freshman year. It was two in the morning, and there was a knock on my dorm room door. I opened it to find this tiny, determined stranger holding a dead phone and asking — very politely, I'll give her that — if she could borrow my charger. She plugged it in, sat down on my floor, and then just… never left. Ten years later, she's still on my floor. Only now there's a ring on her finger and a man next to her who has graciously agreed to share the floor.

For anyone here who has ever tried to make plans with Hannah, you know she is a woman of systems. She has a calendar. She has a backup calendar. She has a spreadsheet for her spreadsheets. When she told me she was planning a wedding, I asked to see the plan, and she sent me a document titled "Wedding — Final — FINAL — v14 — do not edit." I opened it and it was forty-seven pages long. Page thirty-two was a color-coded chart of napkin options. There were four shades that I can only describe as "the same white."

And here's the thing about Hannah, and I say this with love: she is the most generous, loyal, deeply feeling person I have ever met. She is also the kind of person who says "I'm not hungry" and then eats every single fry off your plate. She cries at commercials. All of them. Doesn't matter what it's selling — insurance, cereal, a car with a dog in it. She will cry, and then she will deny crying while actively crying.

But she is also the person who, when my life fell apart in my twenties, drove six hours with a bag of bagels and sat on the floor with me and did not say a single unhelpful thing. She just stayed. That's Hannah. She shows up. She stays.

Which brings me to Andrew.

Now, Andrew — I want to be honest with you, because that's what a maid of honor is for — when Hannah first told me about you, I did my research. I asked questions. I was, let's say, thorough. I needed to know: is this man good enough for my best friend?

And then I watched you two together, and I got my answer. I watched you wait outside a restaurant for fifteen minutes because she texted "almost there" while still at home in her bathrobe. I watched you gently remove her phone from her hand at dinner so she'd actually be present. I watched her laugh at your jokes that aren't funny — and Andrew, they are not funny — and I realized you don't just love Hannah. You *understand* her. You know when she needs to be handled with care and when she needs to be told to stop spiraling and just pick a napkin.

The night they got engaged, Hannah called me at one in the morning — not hysterical, not panicking, which for her is basically a miracle. She said, "Mia, with him, I feel like myself. Only better." And I thought, well, that's the whole thing, isn't it? That's the entire wedding speech right there. I could sit down now. But I have six more minutes.

So here's my one piece of advice, and I promise to keep it brief. Keep being each other's team. Keep saying thank you for the small things — the coffee, the ride, the fact that he takes out those fries you swore you didn't want. Keep laughing at the unfunny jokes, Hannah. Keep being the calm in her storm, Andrew. And on the days when life is not a spreadsheet and nothing is color-coded — because those days are coming — remember you're on the same side.

I also want to thank both families. I've seen the love that raised these two, and looking around this room tonight, it is everywhere.

Hannah, I have loved being your person for ten years. Tonight, I'm very happily handing the job over. Andrew, she's all yours — the calendar, the spreadsheets, the fry-stealing, the cereal commercials. Take good care of her. And Hannah, take good care of him. He waited fifteen minutes outside a restaurant. He's earned it.

So if everyone would please raise a glass — to Hannah and Andrew. To finding the person who makes you feel like yourself, only better. To laughter, to patience, and to a lifetime of arguing over napkins.

To the bride and groom!
